claims.text: Oscillatory-pressure sintering below 1700 °C will refine the microstructure of single-phase ZrB2.
Oscillatory pressure will enhance densification and grain-boundary or inter-particle bonding in single-phase ZrB2.
Enhanced densification and bonding will reduce porosity in the sintered ZrB2 body.
Oscillatory-pressure-sintered ZrB2 will have greater mechanical strength than conventionally high-temperature-sintered ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
Oscillatory-pressure-sintered ZrB2 will have improved oxidation resistance.
Oscillatory-pressure-sintered ZrB2 will have improved liquid plating-metal corrosion durability.
Cyclic mechanical loading at approximately 9 Hz is an applicable oscillatory-sintering parameter for pure ZrB2.
An oxidation exposure near 1300 °C is an applicable test condition for assessing the proposed pure-ZrB2 material.
Periodic pressure perturbations enhance diffusion and consolidation at lower temperature.
The denser, finer-grained structure produced by oscillatory pressure will increase hardness and structural integrity.
Grain refinement will promote formation of a more uniform and protective oxide on ZrB2 during high-temperature exposure.
The refined, dense ZrB2 structure will resist penetration by liquid plating metals.
Sub-1700 °C oscillatory-pressure-sintered ZrB2 will achieve hardness and fracture toughness at least comparable to ZrB2 sintered at or above 2300 °C.
A related Mo-9Si-8B system containing 2.5 wt% ZrB2 and processed by 9 Hz oscillatory sintering showed an 80.3% reduction in oxidation mass loss at 1300 °C.
Adding 2.5 wt% ZrB2 under oscillatory sintering increased the hardness of the cited Mo-9Si-8B alloy.
Adding 2.5 wt% ZrB2 under oscillatory sintering slightly increased the fracture toughness of the cited Mo-9Si-8B alloy.
The cited evidence concerns ZrB2-doped Mo-9Si-8B rather than single-phase ZrB2, making transfer of the reported improvements uncertain.
Prior lower-temperature comparison specimens were prepared at approximately 1700 °C without pressure oscillation.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 specimens require sintering above 2300 °C.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis predicts improved mechanical strength relative to high-temperature ZrB2, whereas the predicted-outcome field requires only properties that are at least comparable; the falsification rule again requires statistically significant improvement. These are materially different success criteria.

The baseline and falsification rule require comparison with both high-temperature ZrB2 and lower-temperature non-oscillatory specimens, but the stated two-set design includes only a high-temperature conventional control and a sub-1700 °C oscillatory group. It omits the required sub-1700 °C non-oscillatory control.
